subject: physics_2
question_text: What are the applications of microwaves?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: the book (p.42) lists exactly two applications — radar and microwave ovens — and both are genuine: radar uses short-wavelength beams that diffract little, and ovens heat food because water molecules absorb microwave energy.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Use in radar
steps.margin_note: First mark. Radar is the standard first application.
steps.why: Microwaves have very short wavelengths, so they diffract little and a radar can send them as a narrow beam toward a target.
common_mistakes: Writing radio waves for radar. Radar uses microwaves because their shorter wavelength keeps the beam narrow.

recall.must_convey: That microwaves are used in radar.

steps.memory_tip: One outdoor use and one kitchen use: radar and the oven.

steps.label: Use in microwave ovens
lines: Microwaves are used in microwave ovens
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The oven takes its name from the waves it uses.
steps.why: Water molecules in food absorb microwave energy, so the food heats through quickly.
common_mistakes: Stopping after one application. The question asks for applications, so give both radar and ovens.

recall.must_convey: That microwaves are used in microwave ovens.

steps.memory_tip: The oven is named after the wave — hard to forget once noticed.

insider_note: Applications is plural — the book marks two, radar and microwave ovens, one mark each.
